descriptionChirho: The compound conjunction כִּי אִם (ki im) functioning as a causal or explanatory particle introducing the reason or ground for a preceding statement, equivalent to 'for, because, surely.' Found in contexts where a speaker provides justification: Gen 15:4 ('this one shall not inherit you, for/surely one from your own body shall inherit you'), Num 35:33, and various prophetic declarations. Rendered as 'fuer/denn' (for/because) in German, 'pour/car' (for/because) in French, 'porque/ciertamente' (because/surely) in Spanish, لِأَنَّ (because) in Arabic, and क्योंकि (because) in Hindi. This causal sense is the foundational meaning from which the adversative and exceptive uses developed through pragmatic strengthening.

The compound conjunction כִּי אִם (ki im) functioning as an adversative or contrastive particle, typically following a negative clause to introduce a correction or contrast: 'not X, but rather Y.' This is the most frequent usage of the compound, appearing in contexts like Gen 32:29 ('your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel'), 1 Sam 8:19, and numerous prophetic texts. Rendered as 'sondern/aber' (but rather/but) in German, 'mais' (but) in French, 'sino/sino que' (but rather) in Spanish, لٰكِنْ/بَلْ (but/rather) in Arabic, and परन्तु/बल्कि (but/rather) in Hindi. The Korean evidence shows the adversative nuance through 오히려 (rather) and 다만 (only/just). This usage presupposes a preceding negation that the כִּי אִם clause then corrects.

The compound conjunction כִּי אִם (ki im) functioning as an exceptive particle meaning 'except, unless, only,' introducing a limitation or exception to a preceding general statement. Found in oath formulas and conditional restrictions: Gen 32:27 ('I will not let you go unless you bless me'), Judg 7:14, Ruth 3:18, and Amos 3:7 ('surely the Lord does nothing except he reveals his counsel'). Rendered as 'ausser/es sei denn' (except/unless) in German, 'sauf/a-moins-que' (except/unless) in French, 'excepto/sino' (except) in Spanish, إِلَّا (except) in Arabic, and सिवाय/जब तक (except/until) in Hindi. The Korean ~하지 않으면 (if not) captures the conditional restriction sense. This exceptive function is syntactically distinct from the adversative because it restricts scope rather than correcting a negation.

The compound conjunction כִּי אִם (ki im) functioning as an emphatic asseverative particle or content clause introducer, meaning 'surely, indeed, that.' This is the least common usage, found in contexts where the speaker makes a solemn affirmation rather than introducing a contrast or exception: Jer 51:14 ('surely I will fill you with men'), and in oath-related contexts where כִּי אִם reinforces the certainty of what follows. Rendered as 'dass/denn' (that/for) in German, 'que/car/ce' (that/for/this) in French, 'que/ciertamente' (that/surely) in Spanish, أَنَّ (that) in Arabic, and कि (that) in Hindi. The Korean 반드시 (certainly) and 참으로 (truly) confirm the asseverative force that distinguishes this from the causal, adversative, and exceptive functions.
